claims.text: High-energy ball milling can produce large-scale Cu–refractory high-entropy alloy composite powders.
The resulting composite powders have a stable, homogeneous microstructure despite the positive heat of mixing.
Repeated fracturing and cold welding during milling force intimate mixing.
Forced intimate mixing during milling hinders macroscopic phase separation.
The proposed initial materials are powders of Cu and refractory alloy constituents such as Mo, Ta, and W.
The proposed intervention is extended-duration high-energy ball milling.
Milling is to be conducted under argon with controlled speed and ball-to-powder ratio, followed by consolidation.
Spark plasma sintering or hot pressing can be used to consolidate the milled powder.
Mechanical alloying overcomes enthalpically unfavorable mixing by forcibly mixing Cu and refractory elements.
The non-equilibrium processing route limits diffusion-driven segregation.
Limiting diffusion-driven segregation helps establish a fine, uniform microstructure.
The Cu–RHEA composite will remain fine-grained and well dispersed at high temperatures.
The composite will exhibit minimal phase separation during consolidation or subsequent thermal exposure.
Without mechanical alloying, direct melting or mixing is hampered by positive mixing enthalpy between Cu and refractory elements.
Direct melting or simple mixing causes macro-segregation and unstable microstructures.
Excessive consolidation temperatures or dwell times can promote partial segregation.
Long-term stability and microstructural refinement depend on milling duration, milling contamination, and consolidation parameters.
